Customer is evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private; main concerns are bursty traffic during live events, data residency, and clear incident recovery behavior. Agreed to run a benchmark and share security docs.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-02-14 09:00 UTC | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Maya Chen, Dev Patel (Redwood) / Alex Romero, Priya Nair, Tom Ellis (Solstice)

[00:00] Maya Chen (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining early um we'll give a quick agenda, hi alex, priya, tom
[00:18] Alex Romero (Solstice): hey maya, thanks. we're pretty pressed to understand how you handle incidents and what fallback behavior looks like for both hosted and dedicated setups
[00:30] Dev Patel (Redwood SE): yeah great, we'll start high level then dig into routing and canary fallbacks, also multi-region options. quick clarification, are you planning live events with spikes?
[00:45] Alex Romero: yes, we have weekly live Q&A streams and then quarterly product launches that spike traffic 5-10x, p95 latency target is around 400ms for single-turn generation, end-to-end 700ms, and we need 99.9 availability during events
[01:10] Priya Nair: and from security we need VPC peering or private deployment to ensure logs never leave our account, plus KMS integration for keys
[01:28] Maya Chen: got it. typical questions: hosted can meet a lot of needs with routed fallbacks, dedicated gives you reserved capacity and predictable throughput, private gives full network control. for hosted we provide multi-region routing and automatic fallback to compatible model variants
[01:50] Tom Ellis: when you say fallback to model variants, does that mean you'll switch to a smaller quantized model if primary is constrained? any risk of hallucination/regression?
[02:05] Dev Patel: yes that's commonly how we do graceful degradation — we route to a lower-cost compatible model or a nearby region. we also attach quality thresholds and can rollback if generation quality dips beyond your eval set. small caveat: quantized swaps can change tokenization edge cases, so we recommend eval prompt sets for your top 50 intents
[02:35] Alex Romero: ok and what about KV cache and prefix caching so that repeated prompts don't blow up costs?
[02:45] Dev Patel: we have KV cache and prefix caching; in hosted we do smart sticky routing so cached prefix hits stay local to the same pool where possible. there are times where routing across regions will necessitate a cold start and you might see latency bumps
[03:05] Priya Nair: for incidents, what's the typical failover time if a region goes down? and do you support active-active multi-region?
[03:18] Maya Chen: we support active-active with health checks. typical failover to a healthy region is sub-30s for routing, warmed KV cache depends — if prefix cache can't be transferred we have burst capacity to handle transient load while cache warms. for dedicated customers we can hot-replicate state depending on topology
[03:40] Tom Ellis: curious about the SLA math — we need an SLA for 99.9 for a service level, but also per-route p95, can you attach SLOs to routes?
[03:55] Dev Patel: yes per-route SLOs are possible in the console, and we can tie alerting to those. SLA for Dedicated includes credit terms; hosted SLAs are lower but we offer SLOs and premium support add-ons
[04:15] Alex Romero: any past incidents we should be aware of, like cross-region outages or fallback mis-routes?
[04:22] Maya Chen: we had a provider-level network issue last year where automatic fallbacks increased latency for a short window — lessons learned: better circuit breaker thresholds, more aggressive canarying, and improved telemetry surfaced in the console. we've since added a circuit breaker that prevents cascading fallbacks
[04:45] Priya Nair: how do you handle audits and logs? we need tamper-evident audit trails and export to our SIEM
[04:55] Dev Patel: we push audit logs to customer-managed sinks for Private, and for Dedicated we can ship to your S3 with enforced retention. hosted supports log export and syslog hooks; all integrate with KMS for encryption at rest
[05:10] Alex Romero: our legal team wants a clear incident playbook: who is the escalation contact, RTO, and postmortem windows
[05:20] Maya Chen: we will include escalation matrix in the security pack. RTO targets depend on deployment — for Dedicated we have explicit RTO commitments, hosted is based on best-effort with premium SLA options
[05:35] Tom Ellis: what about warm standby in a second region? is that extra cost or can Redwood do cold-to-warm on demand?
[05:45] Dev Patel: both options exist. warm-standby reserved pools are additional commit but give near-zero failover latency; cold-to-warm uses burst capacity and can be faster with pre-warmed containers but still has some latency penalty
[06:05] Priya Nair: for encryption, we need customer-managed keys (CMK) in KMS and HSM support for private deployments
[06:15] Maya Chen: yes we support KMS CMK for Dedicated and Private; HSM integrations are available for Private deployments
[06:30] Alex Romero: on network egress, can we enforce geo-residency on model inference so tokens never leave EU for EU customers?
[06:40] Dev Patel: region pinning is supported — you can route EU traffic to EU-only pools, and fallback policies can be configured to avoid cross-region fallbacks if you require strict residency. there is a tradeoff with availability during full-region outage
[07:00] Tom Ellis: tell me about cost impact — if we do multi-region active-active or warm standby, what should we expect cost-wise relative to single region dedicated?
[07:14] Dev Patel: warm standby will add a percent of reserved cost typically 20-40% depending on capacity; active-active doubles some fixed costs but can improve latency. Redwood Optimize can model cost impact given your traffic profile
[07:35] Alex Romero: good. one more — how do you verify fallbacks don't change intent? can we do canary A/B on a small traffic slice?
[07:45] Dev Patel: yes canaries and A/B rollouts are first class; you can run divergence checks against your eval set and automatic rollback if semantic divergence crosses threshold
[08:00] Priya Nair: ok let's talk timeline and pilot. we want a quick POC during our next product event in 6 weeks
[08:07] Maya Chen: that's doable. proposed pilot: 2-week benchmark with your traffic replay, a dedicated small pool for peak slices, and a canary fallback policy. we'll run the benchmark and produce a technical report with latency/cost tradeoffs
[08:25] Tom Ellis: who will own the benchmark run from your side?
[08:30] Dev Patel: SE will own it, I'll put together the script and run with your SRE. we'll need sample traffic and keys sanitized of PHI if any
[08:42] Alex Romero: we'll prepare a redacted traffic dump and share SLOs and top intents
[08:50] [15:00 marker omitted for brevity — call proceeds through technical Q&A and back-and-forth on config]
[30:12] Dev Patel: specific technical note — if you want cross-region cache warming we recommend a hybrid approach: prefix caching plus prefetch hooks at region failover events, sometimes we pre-populate hot keys for known high-volume intents
[31:05] Priya Nair: any compliance gaps for us to know? we are SOC 2 Type II already, would that help shorten onboarding?
[31:14] Maya Chen: yes, our SOC 2 report is available under NDA and will speed security review. for Private deployments we can also provide architecture diagrams and run a short penetration test window
[37:40] Alex Romero: gasping(?) question — how do you guarantee non-retry loops during network blips? we saw cascading retries blow up a system last year
[37:50] Dev Patel: we use rate limiters and circuit breakers at the routing layer, exponential backoff enforced and queuing limits to avoid retry storms. those are configurable per-customer
[41:20] Tom Ellis: ok let's recap next steps
[41:25] Maya Chen: recap: Maya will send SOC 2 + security pack + network diagram; Dev will share benchmark plan and test harness; Priya will share traffic profile and SLOs. action items and due dates captured in the notes. we'll target the pilot week of 2027-02-22.
[41:50] Alex Romero: sounds good, thanks everyone
[41:55] Priya Nair: thanks, we'll ping with the export by Thursday
[42:05] Maya Chen: thanks all, we will follow up with calendar invites for the pilot kickoff and SE deep dive
[52:00] Meeting end: informal sign-off and hangup

Notes: transcript contains occasional ASR errors (e.g., "K-V cash" vs KV cache). References: security pack link (sent after meeting) and benchmark spreadsheet (to be shared by SE).
